“Thus it appears that the sweltering inhabitants of Charleston and New Orleans, of Madras and Bombay and Calcutta, drink at my well.”
_— Henry David Thoreau_



----------View image: (https://media.beehiiv.com/cdn-cgi/image/fit=scale-down,format=auto,onerror=redirect,quality=80/uploads/asset/file/5e76e3cc-e335-4b7b-b059-2573886a647e/image.jpeg?t=1792015227)
Caption: 

# The big business of spare capacity

In the 1830s, India had plenty of things that New Englanders wanted: luxuries like indigo, silk, spices, saltpeter, and cotton textiles.

But the feeling was unrequited. India had no need for New England’s primary exports of dried fish, beaver furs, and whale oil.

As a result, the many ships carrying Indian goods to Boston typically made the return trip to Calcutta entirely empty. Captains had to fill their holds with rocks just to keep their ships from capsizing in the rough seas on the way back.

New England did, however, have an endless supply of one sought-after commodity that India lacked entirely: ice.

Ice cut from the frozen ponds around Boston — including the one Henry David Thoreau made famous — became one of New England’s top exports in the early 19th century. The breakthrough came when Frederic Tudor developed a packing method that kept large blocks of ice from melting too much en route to tropical climates like Charleston, New Orleans, and the Caribbean.

The journey to Calcutta was much longer, of course. But packed tightly and insulated with layers of sawdust, Tudor hoped that most of his ice would survive the trip.

It was worth a try. Even if half of his product melted away, Tudor estimated he’d still be able to make a profit thanks to his negligible shipping costs: ship captains would carry ice to India for almost nothing because it saved them the trouble of filling their holds with rocks.

Tudor’s ice, they reasoned, would serve as ballast.

It worked! The ships stayed afloat, less than half of the ice melted en route, and the remaining ice was sold at a hefty markup to British officials desperate to chill their gin and tonics.

But even with ice selling for six times what it sold for in New England, the venture was only profitable because transportation was essentially free.

This was perhaps the first example of a business built around existing, unused capacity. 

There haven’t been many since.

80841.subject: Uniswap and PancakeSwap Pay LPs More
80841.body:
**gm, Defiers!**

These are the biggest stories in DeFi and crypto:

* **[Richard Heart](https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/richard-heart-detained-in-istanbul-on-interpol-notice-turkish-media-report)**[ was detained in Istanbul](https://thedefiant.io/news/regulation/richard-heart-detained-in-istanbul-on-interpol-notice-turkish-media-report)

* **[Ledger](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/ledger-asks-resellers-to-halt-sales-in-seven-asian-markets)**[ halted sales in seven Asian markets](https://thedefiant.io/news/security/ledger-asks-resellers-to-halt-sales-in-seven-asian-markets)

* **[The EBA](https://thedefiant.io/converge/regulation/eba-names-usdc-the-eu-s-first-significant-e-money-token)**[ named USDC a significant e-money token](https://thedefiant.io/converge/regulation/eba-names-usdc-the-eu-s-first-significant-e-money-token)

* **[U.S. inflation](https://thedefiant.io/news/markets/us-inflation-accelerates-to-3-7-as-gasoline-prices-jump)**[ rose to 3.7% in September](https://thedefiant.io/news/markets/us-inflation-accelerates-to-3-7-as-gasoline-prices-jump)

* **[Babylon](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/babylon-advances-native-bitcoin-collateral-plan-for-aave-v4)**[ proposed native BTC collateral on Aave](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/babylon-advances-native-bitcoin-collateral-plan-for-aave-v4)

A liquidity provider, or LP, deposits two tokens into a decentralized exchange pool so traders can swap between them. The LP earns a share of every swap fee in that pool. Two things cut into that income. The exchange can keep part of each fee for its treasury or token holders. And when prices move on faster markets, arbitrage traders buy from the pool at its old price and keep the gap. Researchers call that second cost loss-versus-rebalancing, or LVR. Today Uniswap and PancakeSwap each changed how much of the fee pool stays with LPs. What did each change, and who pays for it?

Uniswap works on the second cost. Its own protocol still takes part of the first. In July, governance turned on protocol fees for v4 pools, and the v3 fee switch already [took up to a quarter of LP fees](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/uniswap-protocol-revenue-nearly-triples-after-v4-fee-switch-as-uni-tops-usd4) on some tiers. In September, Uniswap Labs [launched StablePair Hook](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/uniswap-launches-dynamic-fees-for-two-stable-pair-pools), which auctions the fee on trades that restore a stablecoin peg. Uniswap [says StablePair pools did $3.1 billion](https://blog.uniswap.org/volatilepair-hook-pricing-both-sides-of-the-trade) in volume in their first four weeks. Today it [launched VolatilePair Hook](https://thedefiant.io/news/defi/uniswap-launches-eth-usdc-pool-with-separate-buy-and-sell-fees) on an ETH/USDC pool. The pool charges different fees for buying and selling ETH, based on recent price moves. After a sharp move, trades that push the price back pay a temporary surcharge. That surcharge returns part of the LVR to LPs.
